brief.title: Senate permitting bill S. 5653 and data center grid costs
brief.summary: S. 5653, the bipartisan permitting package introduced Sept. 30, 2026, would make large computing loads pay more of the cost of transmission. A Grid Strategies estimate puts that at about $55 billion over 10 years. A reported final manager's amendment keeps a 'large loads pay' rule for 20 MW+ loads ahead of a 60-vote cloture vote. That vote's outcome is unknown.
brief.origin:
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito introduced S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, on Sept. 30, 2026, with Sens. Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich. It was referred to Senate Energy and Natural Resources.

The bill has two divisions:
- Division A: NEPA, Clean Water Act and ESA changes, plus 'project certainty' limits on revoking issued permits.
- Division B: transmission sections covering permitting (§2101), planning (§2103), an end to utilities' right of first refusal (§2105), 'ratepayer protection' (§2107), interconnection queue reform (§2110) and data collection on 'computational load entities' (§2114).

On Nov. 2, 2026, TechTarget reported a Grid Strategies estimate that the bill would shift about $55 billion in transmission costs to data centers over 10 years. Around Saturday, Nov. 7, senators reportedly released a final manager's amendment, with a cloture vote set for the following Monday (likely Nov. 9). That report is unconfirmed.
brief.causes:
Data-center demand growth is concentrated in PJM and MISO. It is raising grid investment needs and consumer power bills, which has made 'make data centers pay' a bipartisan affordability message.

The package appears to be a cross-committee deal. Republicans mostly want faster NEPA reviews and fewer lawsuits. Democrats mostly want more transmission and protection for ratepayers. This characterization is the researcher's inference.

States want to keep control over line siting and retail rates. That explains the reported one-year state-first window before FERC's backstop authority applies, and the §2107(b) 'Ratepayer Protection Floor' requiring states to address the generation costs large computing loads create.

actors.name: Sens. Capito, Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich (sponsors)
actors.role: Wrote and sponsor the two-division permitting deal
actors.stake: Passing a bipartisan permitting and transmission package that clears 60 votes

actors.name: FERC
actors.role: Would be directed to revise transmission pricing for large loads; would gain backstop siting authority after the state-review year
actors.stake: Its regulatory scope and workload; the bill also includes FERC staffing provisions

actors.name: States and state utility commissions
actors.role: Get first review of 345 kV+ lines for one year and must address large-load generation costs under §2107(b)
actors.stake: Control over siting and retail rates

actors.name: Data-center developers and hyperscalers
actors.role: Would pay embedded and incremental transmission costs: about $5.5B a year versus about $2B today, per the estimate
actors.stake: Higher grid costs; stronger reasons to accept interruptible service or build on-site generation

actors.name: Utilities
actors.role: Build transmission to serve forecast large loads
actors.stake: Recovering costs if the forecast demand does not show up

actors.name: Grid Strategies (transmission advocates)
actors.stake: New revenue to fund large lines, roughly 10,000 miles of 765 kV

brief.status:
The bill was introduced and referred to committee. A manager's amendment was reportedly released around Nov. 7, 2026. Reported provisions include:
- a one-year state-review requirement for 345 kV+ lines before FERC's backstop applies
- retention of the rule that new loads of 20 MW or more pay the full cost of serving them
- a new DOE Data Center Community Assistance Program

None of these details are verified. The result of the cloture vote (needs 60) is unknown. The $55B figure comes from an advocacy consultancy, not CBO or FERC. About 82% of the cost falls in PJM and MISO, and ERCOT is excluded. The estimate assumes new data centers buy firm transmission service.

research.question: Does making large loads pay embedded plus incremental transmission costs change where data centers locate, and whether they choose firm service, interruptible service or on-site generation?
research.shock: Enactment of S. 5653's large-load cost rule (20 MW+ threshold), if it passes; the Sept. 30, 2026 introduction and Nov. 2026 votes as announcement events
research.data: Interconnection and large-load queues in PJM and MISO (MISO: 163 approved projects, about $11.4B, 43.5 GW of large loads); data-center siting announcements; ERCOT as a comparison region because it is excluded from the estimate

research.question: How should a utility size transmission capacity under uncertain large-load demand when cost-recovery rules shift risk to the loads themselves (capacity planning with demand uncertainty and cost allocation)?
research.shock: The 20 MW+ 'large loads pay' rule versus prior socialized cost allocation
research.data: The Grid Strategies BAAJA white paper; MISO project cost data; utility load forecasts versus realized connections

research.question: Does a one-year state-first review before FERC's backstop change how long high-voltage transmission takes to get permitted?
research.shock: The reported 345 kV+ state-review requirement in the manager's amendment
research.data: Permitting timelines for 345 kV+ lines by state; FERC dockets
